Pele Yoetz 252:1: Letter Nun (continued): Nashim (Women) — Women are obligated in commandments that are not time-bound, like men (see Kiddushin 29a), and there are commandments that, though time-bound, they are nonetheless obligated in, such as the sanctification of Shabbat, the three Shabbat meals, the reading of the Megillah, and all the commandments practiced on the night of Passover, and they are warned regarding all the warnings men are warned about. And now, through our sins, many daughters do not fulfill even the commandments they are obligated in, such as blessings over pleasures, Grace after Meals, prayer, sanctifying the day, the commandment of washing the hands, and keeping Shabbat, and they abound in transgressions since they are talkative, stingy, and given to factionalism, having every bad trait in them, to the point that a mnemonic has been fixed: the orders of Nashim [Women] and Nezikin [Damages, both dealing with quarrels]. And some also cause the public to stumble through the prohibition of improper appearance and evil musings, and other such evils.
Pele Yoetz 252:2: And some are lax about prohibitions because the minds of women are light and lack knowledge and understanding, and they are not expert in blessings, prayers, and the proper order of performing commandments, and they do not know what the prohibitions are and their severity, and the mouth cannot describe the great pitfall under their hands — not out of rebellion or unfaithfulness, God forbid, for in what they do know, they are more careful than men, and what they are lax about and stumble in is due to lack of knowledge, may the good Lord grant them atonement; but this is not a way to remove them from transgression. It is incumbent upon them to go to the women's section and watch from the windows, peering through the lattices to hear teachings, and let woman teach her fellow woman to fear the Lord. And when they are gathered together in a place [that would tempt them] to sing lewd songs and to speak slander, vulgar speech, mockery and other forbidden talk as is their bad custom, let them instead speak the text of prayers and blessings and how the order of serving the Lord goes, and what is the proper order for serving their husbands and raising their children and increasing peace in the home and the like; and let each one take a teacher, male or female, to teach her the text of prayers and the abbreviated Grace after Meals and the blessings over pleasures. And this is a duty incumbent upon the husband, to make expenditures on behalf of his wife, and a father on behalf of his daughter. And how good it would be if they were taught the craft of writing, for then they could easily learn everything.
Pele Yoetz 252:3: And it is also incumbent upon the man to rebuke, uprightly and with a sweet palate, his wife and his daughters and those who accompany him, and draw them away from the whole order of Nezikin [strife], so that all her glory be within, like a king's daughter (Psalms 45:14), modest, watching over the ways of her household (Proverbs 31:27), and thereby a woman who fears the Lord shall be praised (ibid., v. 30). (And if God is with me, I have it in my heart to compile a pamphlet for women covering all the laws pertaining to them and the text of prayers and blessings, all in the vernacular. May the Lord finish this on my behalf and help me for the sake of the honor of His Name, to bring merit to Israel, Amen, so may it be [His] will.)
Pele Yoetz 252:4: And the wives of Torah scholars especially must be careful of every hint of transgression, since others learn from them to be lenient about prohibitions, and there is also a desecration of the Name involved. Likewise they must conduct themselves with good and upright traits to an even greater degree, watching over the ways of her household, and should not be particular at all about the beauty of clothing and jewelry, for it is enough that she has a share in her husband's Torah, which is more precious than pearls and beyond all treasures; rather, let her be a help to her husband to serve the Lord and engage in Torah, and not burden him with her questions, and let her rise while it is still night and make preparations, and be a wife who converses with her husband, [saying,] “Arise, cry out to your God.” And let all the wife's aim be to help her husband in Torah and service, and let her devote herself to this with pleasant speech, grace and honor. And let her also keep her eyes open regarding her children, for this duty is incumbent upon her even more, since she is present in the home, and also because this is her portion. And in what do these women merit reward? By having their husbands and sons read [Torah], etc., and thereby they merit the great promise that the Holy One, blessed be He, promised women (Berachot 17a), for greater is one who causes [others to do a mitzvah] than one who does it himself.
Pele Yoetz 253:1: Nefilat Apayim (Falling on One's Face) — There are many merits to intending properly in falling on one's face [i.e., the Tachanun prayer], as brought in the book “Devash LePi” (entry Nun, letter 1), and it is summarized at length there, in these words: they wrote in the name of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, that one who has proper intention during falling on one's face merits many virtues. One, that he becomes like a new creature, as though he had already died, for his soul ascends to God in complete surrender with all his heart. Two, they give him strength and vigor to fight the evil inclination. Three, additional understanding in Torah and its secrets. Four, additional cleaving to his Maker. Five, he merits the path that guides him when he departs from the world. Six, it causes an influx of blessing to the Divine Presence. Seven, no sin comes about through him, and if it happens that he sins, he will be afflicted in this world until the sin is purged — this is a brief summary of his words. And who has seen such things and would not give his soul with all his strength to have proper intention as is fitting? And every person is obligated only according to his own measure, as far as his understanding reaches, and let him do whatever is in his power to do.
Pele Yoetz 253:2: And if he knows it by heart, he should perform the falling on his face on his left arm, and intend with all his heart, and especially when saying “To You, O Lord, I lift up my soul,” he should be very careful to intend with all his heart that he is ready to give his life for the sanctification of the Lord's Name should the opportunity arise, for they said in the holy Zohar (part 3, p. 121 approx.) that one who does not have this intention causes himself to depart from the world before his days are complete, Heaven have mercy. Therefore, whoever desires life should intend with all his heart every day, and also intend that the work of our hands establish for us [our worthiness], for these matters are ancient, exceedingly deep, and stand at the summit of the world. And this is a great principle in all blessings, commandments, prayers, and studies: behold, a ladder set up on the earth with its top reaching to the heavens.
Pele Yoetz 254:1: Niflaot (Wonders) — One who mentions His wonders, blessed be He, is saved from trouble because of this. And they said in Shocher Tov (Psalm 70): the Holy One, blessed be He, redeemed Israel and performed miracles for them only because they used to mention His wonders. David said, “If so, I shall mention them, and You shall save me.” Up to here, the words of our sages, of blessed memory, brought in the book Devash LePi (entry Nun, letter 5). Thus, how good and pleasant it is to read the book of Psalms, applying one's mind to know what he is saying, and how good is a word fitly spoken — that he tell of the wonders and mention the kindnesses of the Lord to his wife and household on Passover, Chanukah, Purim and the like. Likewise, when standing among gatherings in synagogues of people who take pleasure in excessive talk, instead of speaking idle and forbidden words and the like, let the God-fearing man, recalling the verse (Malachi 2:17), “You have wearied the Lord with your words,” turn the conversation to telling of the wonders of the Lord that He did for Israel in general and for himself and others in particular, and from him they will see and do likewise, and all will tell of His righteousness and His wonders, blessed be He, and thus the Name of Heaven is magnified, and this is a commandment for which reward is received.
Pele Yoetz 255:1: Ner Shabbat V'Ner Chanukah (The Shabbat Candle and the Chanukah Candle) — The saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Shabbat 23b), that one who is careful with them merits sons who are Torah scholars. And the matter of this carefulness is that the vessel used for lighting should be beautiful and clean, and that one should light with pure olive oil, and on Shabbat should increase the number of candles, and how good it would be to light a lamp with seven wicks. And they wrote in the name of the Ari, of blessed memory, that trimming the wicks should be done by the man, and the lighting by the woman. And if for all commandments it is fitting for a person to strengthen himself to fulfill the commandment with the choicest, to give delight to his Creator, how much more so for commandments such as these, whose reward comes with good reward, for a man gives all the wealth of his house with love in order to merit for his children the crown of Torah. And I am accustomed to say before lighting the Chanukah candle:
Pele Yoetz 255:2: “For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, I am hereby ready and prepared to fulfill the commandment of lighting the Chanukah candle, as our sages, of blessed memory, instituted for us. May it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our fathers, that it be considered before You as though we had intended with all the proper intentions, and may our commandment of lighting the Chanukah candle rise before You together with the commandment of lighting the Chanukah candle of Your children who know and intend with all the proper intentions. And by the power of the special virtue of the commandment of lighting the Chanukah candle, grant us and our offspring the merit of the candle of the commandment and the light of Torah, and may they illuminate and complete the two hundred forty-eight limbs of our soul, our spirit and our neshamah, and may the Temple be rebuilt speedily in our days, and there we shall light the Menorah through Your holy kohanim. And just as You performed miracles for our ancestors, so now save us and gather us and rescue us from the nations, to give thanks to Your Name, to praise Your glory, if not by merit — by mercy, and in Your abundant mercies may You desire us and be pleased with us. And may the pleasantness of the Lord be upon us,” etc.
Pele Yoetz 256:1: Letter Samech: Savlanut (Patience) — How good and pleasant is patience! This good trait is needed by every person — the great according to his greatness, the small according to his smallness. If he is a head over the community, he must bear the burden of the people, and bear the insults of worthless men who defy him, and lead and guide them with a spirit of calm; likewise, every man in his own household, regarding his wife and child — always let the left hand push away and the right hand draw near, all according to what the person is, and according to the child's understanding and age, his traits, the occasion and the need. A scale and balance of judgment is needed, and weighing the matter with the holy shekel, which is the straight path — whether to cast bile or to bear and be silent, whether to speak gently or harshly. And how much strength is needed to bear in the matter of speech, as the sage said, “Before you speak the word, you are its master; once you have spoken it, it is your master” (Sefer Chasidim, section 86). Therefore, even if his heart burns like fire and speech churns within him wanting to burst out, let him be firm like a lion in subduing his inclination and hold back with words, for truly they said, “A word is worth a sela, silence two” (Megillah 18a), and “patience, patience — it is worth four hundred zuz” (Berachot 20a). And especially at a time of anger, he should make himself like a mute, not opening his mouth, for “not with knowledge does he speak, and a man of anger stirs up strife with his words,” and he curses and reviles, and even the Divine Presence is not considered before him [i.e., he shows no reverence]. Therefore silence is best, and he should bear it and not respond to the one who reviles him, for one who guards his mouth and tongue guards his soul from distress (Proverbs 21:23), and merits abundant good.
Pele Yoetz 256:2: And how much patience is needed by one who wishes to be a teacher of Torah to schoolchildren, or to his own children, who are sometimes difficult to listen and quick to forget, either because they lack understanding, or because they do not pay attention to listen and understand, and it is human nature to become angry as well; patience is needed to rebuke them as is fitting for them according to what they are, and to guide them, and to repeat with them again and again, as in the story of Rabbi Preida, who used to review with his student four hundred times and merited good reward (Eruvin 54b). Let the wise man hear and add learning (ibid. 54a-b approx.). Likewise, whoever's lot has fallen to a bad portion, a difficult-tempered wife, let him be firm in strengthening himself to bear it all for the sake of peace in the home, for it is great. And it is no praise for one whom everyone honors and exalts and does his will as he pleases that he does not become angry; rather, one may truly boast when they anger him to his face and treat him improperly, and he bears it all and forgoes his own grievance, for by this he gains that all his transgressions are overlooked for him. And the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, is known (Chullin 89a) on the verse “He hangs the earth on nothing [belimah]” (Job 26:7), that the world endures on account of one who restrains [bolem] his mouth at a time of quarrel. And everyone in the world knows that patience is very good, but they say, who is the man who can bear it? However, given its severity and the benefit that follows from it for body and soul in this world and the World to Come, it is fitting to be firm in strengthening oneself with great vigor, and whatever a man desires to do, he can do with the help of the Almighty, and the reward is according to the pain, and one who comes to purify himself is helped [from Heaven].
Pele Yoetz 257:1: Sukkah — The sukkah is an important and beloved commandment that comes from time to time, and happy is Israel, most of whom are careful and make a beautiful sukkah with beautiful furnishings — happy is their portion. But there are frivolous people who, in order not to trouble themselves a little, and because they worry about their bellies, refrain from making a sukkah and rely on the community sukkah, where they eat an olive's volume on the first two nights. And even those who make a sukkah, some are lenient and sit in it only occasionally, eating and sleeping outside the sukkah. Would that they gain wisdom to understand how beloved this commandment is, both according to the plain meaning — that it stands for a person as an atonement in place of exile — and according to the esoteric meaning, whose mysteries are exceedingly lofty; and the little our understanding has grasped is that the Divine Presence spreads its wings over us, like a mother crouching over her chicks, and seven supernal guests, the light of the sparks of their souls, dwell there, for which reason its sanctity is as great as the sanctity of the synagogue, and for this reason they forbade treating it with disrespect, and certainly forbade laughter and levity in it. And they said of the Ari, of blessed memory, that he was careful not to speak mundane talk inside the sukkah. And certainly one who is careful to establish his dwelling and residence in it for all seven days in holiness and purity, with awe and fear and great joy, as is proper, acquires holiness and additional illumination in his soul, spirit and neshamah, and finds means of redemption for the whole year to serve his Creator with complete service.
Pele Yoetz 257:2: There are also other commandments accompanying and performed during the festival of Sukkot, such as taking the lulav and performing the wavings during the blessing and during Hallel, and circling the reader's table while reciting Hoshanot with the four species in hand — these are matters that stand at the summit of the world, yet people treat them with disrespect. There are places where even one who can afford to obtain a lulav for himself does not do so, relying instead on the community's lulav, and even one who does take a lulav does not perform the wavings, thinking this is merely a custom of the sages and the pious and not knowing that this is the essence of the commandment, for we have learned (Sukkah 42b) that a minor who knows how to wave, his father buys him a lulav, and we have also learned (ibid. 37b) where they wave — at “Hodu” and at “Ana,” and we have learned that every day they used to circle the altar, etc. (ibid. 45a). And the man who fears the Lord and greatly delights in His commandments should strive with all his strength and all his might to have his own lulav of the choicest quality, and should give thought to this from the beginning of the year, sending far and wide to several places so that he not lack a lulav and etrog, for it is a beloved commandment and a good sign for the whole year, and he should not refrain from performing the wavings and circling the table. But if he cannot afford to have his own lulav, let him strive to perform the wavings and circle the table with his neighbor's lulav sitting near him, and should not worry about the mockery of the complacent, for if he could find a way to earn a thousand thousand gold coins, he would not refrain from earning them because of the mockery of the complacent — how much more so to do the will of our Father in Heaven, who gives good reward to those who do His will. This is a great principle in the Torah: if you seek it as silver, then you will understand the fear of the Lord.
Pele Yoetz 257:3: There is also included in this holy festival the commandment of the joy of a commandment. And if on every pilgrimage festival it is a commandment to rejoice, how much more so on this holy festival, which is the time of our rejoicing, as we say in prayer, and of which it is written (Deuteronomy 16:14-15), “And you shall rejoice in your festival,” and “you shall be altogether joyful.” However, our Maker commanded us only regarding joy of the heart, that one be satisfied and full of the joy of a commandment, as a living person takes to heart: what are we and what is our life, and how good is our portion and how pleasant our lot, that our Maker chose us and has never ceased to cherish us, and an extraordinary, boundless affection is known to us, beyond our comprehension. And the little our own eyes see is that He counseled us well and gave us Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur to atone for our sins through them, and in His love and compassion, as a father delights in a son, He wished to gladden us from our grief and pain that we suffered during the days of repentance, and gave us immediately the festival of Sukkot, commanding us to rejoice and fixing good reward for our joy. Is there anything sweeter than this? And the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to bring merit to Israel, therefore He gave them abundant Torah and commandments (Makkot 23b), and gave us the commandment of the sukkah to spread the shelter of His peace over us, and the commandment of the four species of the lulav, which are a good sign for Israel and a raising of a banner to show that we are the victors, as our sages, of blessed memory, said in the midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 30:4), a parable of two who came for judgment, etc. And He commanded us to rejoice with the joy of a commandment, and this is a good sign for the whole year, as the disciples of the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote: whoever is joyful and glad of heart and does not grieve at all during this holy festival is assured that a good year will come to him and that he will be joyful forever.
Pele Yoetz 257:4: Therefore let a man be firm in strengthening himself to forget his sadness, his anger, and everything that pains him, and to rejoice every day with a new joy, the joy of a commandment, as is written in the holy Zohar (Vayikra, p. 56), by persisting in pure thoughts as stated. And beyond this, there is even more room to rejoice when he takes to heart what is accomplished in Heaven above through him — happy is one born of woman who has merited this, to build his chambers in heaven: “What is man that You are mindful of him... You have given him dominion over the works of Your hands, You have put all things under his feet.” This and more should the living take to heart and be aroused and say aloud, “It is impossible not to rejoice,” and raise his voice to sing and chant the prayers, Hallel, songs and praises with a voice of joyous song and thanksgiving, a celebrating multitude. And let it be remembered that when the Temple stood, the righteous and pious used to increase the joy of the Water-Drawing Celebration, and whoever had not seen this joy had never in his life seen [true] joy, and through this they drew forth the holy spirit; and certainly great is the pain of Heaven that through our sins our city has been destroyed, etc., and the Lord shall roar from on high (Jeremiah 25:30), etc. This is the comfort of our Father in Heaven and our comfort in our affliction — that our Father in Heaven still holds His affection over us, leaping over the mountains, skipping over the hills, watching from the windows, peering through the lattices to see the joy of His children in the synagogues, as it is written in the holy Zohar (part 3, p. 114 approx.). Therefore let Israel rejoice in its Maker with the joy of a commandment, not the joy of levity in the manner of fools who drink much wine from their winepresses and raise their voices with the remnants of gentile song — this is not joy but levity, and this is not a commandment but a transgression, and though they do it in the name of a commandment, it is a transgression in their hands; may the good Lord grant atonement for it.
Pele Yoetz 257:5: And in his own joy, let him mix in gladdening the hearts of the poor and needy, for this is the commandment of all festivals and holidays — for if he rejoices but does not rejoice the poor, of him it is written (Malachi 2:3), “And I will spread dung upon your faces, the dung of your festivals.” And all the more so on this holy festival, it is incumbent upon him to give the poor a share of the guests' portion, for if he does not give, the [supernal] guests curse him with fierce curses, and if he gives, he receives abundant blessings from them, as explained in the holy Zohar (part 3, p. 104 approx.). Therefore let a man tremble and take hold of himself, and desire blessing, and not refrain from inviting some poor person to his table; and if he cannot do this, let him at least set aside from his money for charity on the eve of the festival for each meal, and say aloud, “This I give to charity for the sake of the portion of Abraham, the holy guest,” and “this I give for the sake of the portion of Isaac, the holy guest,” from my meal, and so on in this manner; or let him send food to a poor person before each meal, and thereby he will receive blessing and abundant good.
Pele Yoetz 258:1: Syag (Fence) — The Torah itself commanded a fence for the Torah, as it is said (Leviticus 18:30), “And you shall keep My charge” — make a safeguard for My charge (Mo'ed Katan 5a). And our holy sages have already made fences and safeguards firmly fixed like nails, for the words of the Sages are more stringent than the words of the Torah (Yerushalmi Berachot 1:4; Avodah Zarah 2:7). However, it is not fitting to reveal to unlearned people the reason for a prohibition being merely to prevent them from transgressing the words of the Torah and the like, for one who is frivolous will say, “I have no need of a fence, since it is not forbidden by the Torah,” not knowing, in their confusion of spirit, that once a matter has come from the mouths of the Sages, we are bound by the prohibition of “do not deviate,” and even if he does not transgress the words of the Torah, since he transgresses the words of the Sages alone, he is liable to death and is judged with boiling excrement, Heaven have mercy (Eruvin 21b).
Pele Yoetz 258:2: And for another reason as well I say that it is not fitting to reveal to unlearned people which prohibitions are rabbinic and their reasons and rationale, lest they come to be lenient according to their limited and false understanding. And I have seen with my own eyes a man who was somewhat God-fearing and was careful not to eat cheese milked by a gentile unsupervised by a Jew, but would take the milk and curdle it himself at home and eat it, saying, “Since they permitted gentiles' butter and the like because impure milk does not curdle, I too shall do likewise.” But he did not understand the reasoning, that specifically when the gentile himself curdles it, we are not concerned about a mixture of impure milk, since it makes no difference to him [the gentile], as he does not know it won't curdle; but when he sells milk to a Jew, there is a possibility that some impure milk is mixed in and remains in the residue of the milk. Likewise there are ignorant people who are lenient about eating a gentile's milk, saying, “What is the reason if not the concern about impure milk? I am confident that no impure milk is mixed in it.” And so it goes in several other prohibitions, being lenient with false burdens, deceptions and arguments of the evil inclination. Therefore, for the honor of God, conceal the matter in these cases without telling them that the prohibition is rabbinic, with its reason and rationale, and simply tell them, “This is a great sin, this is a criminal sin,” so that they listen and fear.
Pele Yoetz 258:3: And there is yet another reason not to reveal to unlearned people that a prohibition is rabbinic: lest they come to complain and speak ill of our holy sages, saying, “How they have burdened the yoke upon us, forbidding us many decrees and prohibitions beyond what the Torah forbade!” not knowing that were it not for the words of the Sages, the words of the Torah would not endure, and would that they had decreed even more upon us — we would have needed it. Do you not see that because they permitted us to carry an object in the marketplace on Shabbat in a city surrounded by a wall by means of an eruv, there are places where many unlearned people are lenient enough to carry even in a city not surrounded by a wall, or outside the wall; and because they permitted charging interest by means of a business contract [heter iska], some are lenient even without a contract and take fixed interest. And through our many sins, there are several matters where leniency leads to prohibition, and it would have been fitting for them to be forbidden even more, except that they did not wish to decree unless the majority of the community could bear it, and moreover, all their words were spoken with divine inspiration and have a root above. Do you not see, in the two pairs of tefillin we lay, of Rashi and of Rabbeinu Tam, how lofty their mysteries are, exalted on high! Likewise the second day of festivals observed in the Diaspora, and all their words are matters that stand at the summit of the world, and all were said to Moses at Sinai, and to them nothing is to be added and from them nothing is to be subtracted. And this is the teaching for man: each person should build for himself, or for the people of his city and locality, fences and safeguards according to what he is and according to the need of the hour, and wage war with strategies against the evil inclination, and flee a hundred gates of the permitted so as not to enter even one gate of the forbidden, and thereby he fulfills what the Torah said (Leviticus 18:30), “And you shall keep My charge.” And when the Lord sees the ways of a man who wishes to be helped and saved from the evil inclination, the Holy One, blessed be He, rejoices, and the Lord will not abandon him into his hand, and will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 258:4: And the Rambam, of blessed memory, has already written (Hilchot De'ot, ch. 2, halachah 2) that although the straight path a person should choose is a complete middle path, nevertheless, if one is accustomed to some transgression or some bad trait, it is fitting for him to distance himself from one extreme to the other until he arrives at the middle path — such as one accustomed to drunkenness, which is a great evil that destroys both soul and body, he should accustom himself for extended periods not to drink at all except for Kiddush and Havdalah; and likewise, if one is accustomed by nature to be lazy, he should strengthen himself to be quick and diligent until his nature is reversed, for it is within a person's power to reverse his nature, and habit becomes a second nature. And this is the whole of man: that he strive with all his strength, day by day, to straighten his traits and his ways, and to change his nature — let it be exchanged, let it be traded, evil for good, through strategies, fences, safeguards, penalties and the like, for the reward is according to the pain (Avot, end of ch. 5). And regarding this I have heard it said, as a hint, an interpretation of the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Megillah 28b), that whoever reviews halachot every day is assured of being destined for the World to Come — meaning that one who changes [i.e., corrects] his ways every day, going back and forth, going and growing, is assured of being destined for the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 259:1: Sod (Mystery/Esoteric Wisdom) — The study of the mysteries of the Torah is exceedingly lofty above all other studies. Happy is he whom the Lord has granted a share in understanding, who has a hand and a name in the wisdom of Kabbalah, and who intends [the Kabbalistic meanings] in performing commandments, in his prayers, and in his study, according to the esoteric meaning. How good is his portion and how pleasant his lot — the mouth cannot describe the greatness of their virtue. And one accustomed to the holy book of the Zohar will indeed see the great virtue of these complete men, wondrous and astonishing. And one who has no hand in this wisdom, his evil is great, to the point that they said (Zohar part 3, p. 141 approx.), “Whoever did not enter and did not exit — it would have been better for him not to have been created,” and many such sayings that embitter the heart. And certainly the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal tyrannically with His creatures, and every person is obligated only according to his own measure, and Scripture speaks of what is possible.
Pele Yoetz 259:2: Thus it is incumbent upon every Torah scholar, after he has filled his stomach with Talmud and halachic authorities, to turn himself to walk in the orchard [of Kabbalah], and strive with great vigor, as the good hand of the Lord is upon him, to enter this wisdom; and he must first fulfill the conditions required for this wisdom, as explained in the introduction to “Eitz HaChaim” by our teacher Rabbi Chaim Vital, and in the responsa “Chavot Yair,” and in other books of the Kabbalists, and then the mysteries of the Torah will be made easy for him and he will become like an overflowing spring, and let him bear the burden and not wilt in order to merit this wisdom, for his honor is great in Heaven above, since he gives great delight to his Creator. And one accustomed to the book of the Zohar, the Tikkunim, and the books of the Kabbalists will see with his eyes and his heart will understand the great virtue of this wisdom, and will give his life for it, for the reward is according to the pain.
Pele Yoetz 259:3: And indeed, even one who has no hand in this wisdom should not refrain from perusing the books of the Kabbalists that explain the intent of prayers, blessings and commandments according to the esoteric meaning, for then, at the time of performing them, his heart will be inflamed as he recalls that these are matters that stand at the summit of the world, exceedingly deep and exalted on high. Happy is one born of woman who builds his chambers in heaven, and let him not serve in his prayer to receive a reward, but rather intend to repair matters at their root, for the sake of the knowledge of the holy ones who are in the land, the mighty ones in whom is all my delight, and let his heart cry out to his Father that the work of our hands be established for us.
Pele Yoetz 259:4: And one who looks into the books of the Kabbalists will understand in his heart a little that great is our Master and His greatness is beyond measure (Psalms 145:3), and will understand a little how great is the blemish caused by the sinner, and what great blemish and damage every single transgression causes, and how greatly the evil of the destruction of the Temple, which our many sins caused, in such a way that it is fitting for a person to be embittered upon recalling these things, and to shed tears like a river without ceasing. And correspondingly, one who understands will understand what is accomplished in Heaven above through our prayers, our commandments and our studies, and on Shabbatot and Rosh Chodesh and festivals and holidays, in such a way that Israel shall rejoice in its Maker with joy and gladness of heart more than from great abundance. In sum, they said that whoever has not tasted this wisdom has not tasted the taste of the fear of sin, and of serving God with fear and love and great joy, as is proper.
Pele Yoetz 259:5: And one who accustoms himself to gaze upon the pleasantness of the books of the Kabbalists will see with his own eyes that there is nothing empty of it — even in eating and drinking and other clothing and conjugal relations, and the ways of a husband's affection for his wife and the like, and even in going outside, in everything there are supernal mysteries and worlds being built, provided one does the things properly, without any trace of prohibition, and directs his heart toward Heaven. Happy are we, how good is our portion! Therefore it is good for a man to conduct himself to fulfill everything according to the esoteric meaning, in the manner of the pious, and even though he does not know the esoteric meaning, [let him trust that] the work of our hands is established for us and gives delight to our Creator.
Pele Yoetz 259:6: And a person must be trustworthy in spirit, concealing a matter, and not reveal his secret to every person, for wisdom is with the discreet (Proverbs 1:2). Even regarding mundane matters, it is already written in the Book of Ben Sira: “Many will be those who seek your peace; reveal your secret to but one in a thousand” (Yevamot 63b). And I say that even to this one, he should reveal it only out of necessity, such as to seek counsel and the like, for they said, “Do not reveal to your friend what you conceal from your enemy,” unless you have tested him many times and found him a trustworthy friend, lest he turn into your enemy and reveal your secret. And go and learn how careful one must be that his secret not be revealed, from our father Jacob, peace be upon him, as it is written (Genesis 31:4), “And Jacob sent and called Rachel and Leah to the field, to his flock,” and our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 8b, with Rashi, see there) — from here we learn that a person should not speak a secret matter in the house, but rather in an open place, since walls have ears. And greater than this we find with our holy Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi], who would not speak of the secret matters he had with Antoninus except by way of hint, since a bird of the sky may carry the word (Avodah Zarah 10a). And the well-known story of Baba ben Buta's servant with Herod (Bava Batra 4a) is known. Thus how greatly one must be careful when speaking secret matters with members of his household, for sometimes people are told what was said, whether through walls having ears, or because of listeners, or children in the house, who are talebearers revealing secrets (Proverbs 1:13, approx. wording), and a sword and great evil result; and one who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from distress (ibid. 21:23).
Pele Yoetz 259:7: And one must be very careful not to reveal his fellow's secret to any person — even to one's wife they said this — and even if he [the one entrusted] instructs and says “do not reveal it,” for his fellow too will do as he did and reveal it to another on condition that he not reveal it, and in the end the matter becomes known. And they said in the Idra Kadisha that whoever reveals mysteries is as though he diminishes men and as though he worships idolatry. And a hint for this is established: one who reveals mysteries — it is known that his soul is not from the body of the holy King, and therefore he has no [portion in] mystery, and when his soul departs it does not cling to the body of the King, since that is not its place. Woe to that person, woe to him, woe to his soul — this is a brief summary of the words of the holy Zohar (Parashat Ha'azinu, p. 294 approx.). Let a man tremble and take hold of himself and not reveal his fellow's secret. And this applies not only when told in confidence, but even anything not explicitly permitted to be told falls under the prohibition of “it shall not be told,” as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 4b), and many times a person speaks his words with relatives and acquaintances without worrying to instruct them not to reveal it, and they go and tell things outside, and a sword results. Look and see what happened to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, peace be upon him, when Rabbi Yehudah ben Gerim went and told things outside, and go see what came of it (Shabbat 33a).
Pele Yoetz 259:8: Thus, silence is the remedy for everything, and how much disgrace, harm and prohibition befalls those who dig and search to know another's secret by listening behind a wall, or by deception, or by opening letters. And the ban of Rabbeinu Gershom, Light of the Exile, of blessed memory, is known. And it is already written in the responsa Halachot Ketanot (part 1, section 276) that one who digs to know another's secret transgresses “you shall not go about as a talebearer among your people” (Leviticus 19:16), for what difference does it make to him whether he reveals his fellow's secret to another or to himself — from this too comes a sword, hatred and strife, and the flame of the fire of discord rises with no remedy. Therefore let one who guards his soul distance himself from all these, for whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord, and happy are the innocent of way.
Pele Yoetz 260:1: Sefer (A [Torah] Book/Scroll) — It is known that one of the six hundred thirteen commandments is for each Israelite to write a Torah scroll for himself. And whoever the Lord has graced with the ability should not fail to fulfill this commandment, for they said in the holy Zohar (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 70, p. 132 approx.) that even for a single commandment that one could fulfill and does not fulfill, he must return to fulfill it in a transmigration, and Scripture says (Deuteronomy 27:26), “Cursed be he who does not uphold the words of this Torah to do them.” And although the halachic authorities have written (Tur, Yoreh De'ah, near sec. 270) that in this age the essence of the commandment is to buy books of halachic authorities and Torah commentaries, nevertheless, according to the mystical meaning of the matter, it is obviously incumbent upon one to write a valid Torah scroll, and Heaven forbid that any commandment be nullified or exchanged, for the God of knowledge, the Lord, foresees and beholds to the end of all generations, and nevertheless commanded us this commandment for now and for generations, and the matters are ancient and exceedingly deep — who can fathom them? Know that if this commandment were merely so that one have it and read from it alone, any book would suffice — why then was the Omnipresent particular that the writing be on parchment and with ink, and there are several matters that are a law given to Moses at Sinai that invalidate a Torah scroll? Rather, certainly all this is according to the mystical meaning of the matter, which stands at the summit of the world.
Pele Yoetz 260:2: And from what has been said, you shall hear that those who buy a Torah scroll in partnership, or members of a group who buy a Torah scroll and give it to the synagogue, have accomplished nothing toward fulfilling the commandment of writing a Torah scroll, for this commandment is that each person write a Torah scroll for himself. Would that their hearts had been set on spending those expenditures on other, more important commandments, for one who makes expenditures on commandments must weigh the reward of the commandment, like a good merchant who seeks to spend his money and invest it in merchandise that yields great profit. And they already said in the Yerushalmi (Shekalim, end of ch. 5) that Rabbi so-and-so and Rabbi so-and-so were walking in a place where there were synagogues. One said to his companion, “How much money my ancestors sank here!” The other said to him, “How many souls your ancestors sank here — were there not people who could have occupied themselves with Torah [with that money]?” From this you may deduce regarding the many expenditures that donors among the people make in the name of a commandment, without knowledge or understanding to choose, with that money, many honorable commandments instead. Thus, it is good for a man to take counsel with his Maker or with a Torah scholar, and choose and distinguish between good and better; and if the Lord widens his boundary so that his hand can afford everything, let him hold to this and not let go of that either, and how good is a word fitly spoken, for they have written (Midbar Kedumot, entry Samech) that one who gives the synagogue a new Torah scroll on Shavuot is as though he offered a new meal-offering to the Lord in its proper time.
Pele Yoetz 260:3: And included in this is that he should also hold to buying books, and not let go of buying a Torah scroll either, for buying books is a great principle in the Torah. For a Torah scholar, they already said that just as there is no craftsman without tools, so there is no scholar without books, and books are our eyes, without which a person cannot lift his hand to render rulings and judge cases. And for the rest of the people, every person is obligated, according to his own measure, to buy many books of Torah commentaries, ethical books, and books of law for those who know the Holy Tongue, and in the vernacular for those who speak other languages, and books of the Bible, Mishnayot, the holy Zohar and the like, and it is fitting to pursue them as one pursues a partridge in the mountains, and not to worry about the cost, for the love of the blessed Name is as mighty as death, and is attained only through love of the Torah, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Kiddushin 30b), “I have created the evil inclination, I have created for it the Torah as a remedy,” and Scripture says (Deuteronomy 30:12), “It [the Torah] is not in heaven,” nor “beyond the sea,” and our sages, of blessed memory, said (Eruvin 55a), “This implies that had it been in heaven or beyond the sea, you would have had to go after it.”
Pele Yoetz 260:4: Therefore his heart should not find it difficult to spend money and gold to buy many books, fulfilling the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Proverbs 23:23), “Buy truth and do not sell it,” and even if he has books he does not know how to read, or has duplicates, he should not sell them unless it is in order to buy others in their place, for it is written in Sefer Chasidim: a story of one who had an extra copy of the book of the Zohar and sold it, and in his dream they called him “Beheimah” [beast], and they told him that the initial letters of “beheimah” mean “want to remove a holy congregation from the house” [an acronym]. Not only this, but he should also buy some books and lend them to others, for regarding this our sages, of blessed memory, said (Ketubot 50a) that of him it is said, “Wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness stands forever” (Psalms 112:3). And they said in the midrash that as a reward for this commandment one merits male children. And it is fitting that this protect him so that he have descendants who are wise men who study from them, but the Torah should not be set as an offering in a corner to rot and gather dust; rather, let him lend them so that others study from them, and take a receipt from them as evidence in his hand, and the merit of the students depends on him.
Pele Yoetz 260:5: And a person is obligated to keep his books in good condition and shake the dust off them from time to time, and to treat them with great honor, holding them respectfully and setting them properly in their place, and not to treat them disrespectfully, God forbid, for one who disrespects them disrespects the word of the Lord, God forbid, for they are considered the King's garments, and whoever honors the Torah is himself honored (Avot 4:5; Avot DeRabbi Natan 27a), and this is what grants him the merit to attain the crown of Torah. And part of the honor due to books is that one should not write idle words on the page or in the margin as foolish youths are accustomed to do, and should not lean on a book, and should not place them on the ground beneath him, and all similar things. The general rule of the matter is: whoever increases the honor of books for the honor of Heaven, his own honor is increased.
Pele Yoetz 260:6: And how good and pleasant it is to say all prayers and all blessings from the book, for this helps one focus on what he is saying. And a mnemonic is fixed: “say [it] with the book, his bad thoughts will turn back.” And especially in the Amidah prayer, if one does not pray with closed eyes, it is incumbent upon him to keep his eyes on the book and not let his eyes wander here and there, for they were strict in the holy Zohar (Devarim, p. 254 approx.) about its punishment, and it is a disgraceful thing, and by this a person is recognized, whether he is an ignoramus or God-fearing.
Pele Yoetz 260:7: And it is fitting for a person to strive to receive an aliyah to the Torah, and to rejoice greatly when he goes up to the Torah. And they have written that by this he acquires illumination in his soul, and he should not be particular about the place of the aliyah which, in his opinion, is not befitting his honor, for this too is vanity and vexation of spirit; and if he is honored in another congregation with an aliyah to the Torah, let him go, for the honor of the Torah, for if he does not go, it is possible he is included among those of whom they said (Berachot 55a) that whoever is given a Torah scroll to read and does not read, his days are shortened, Heaven have mercy — unless there is some strong reason not to go. In any case, let him strive to pay for the aliyah [i.e., not lose out on this good deed] and not lose much good.
Pele Yoetz 260:8: And it is known that it is incumbent upon one called up to the Torah to recite the blessings properly, aloud, and many unlearned people err in this — woe to that shame, to show before the congregation and assembly that they do not know the blessings for the Torah, with no one taking it to heart to learn, but rather saying them in a whisper to cover their shame, and according to many halachic authorities (Orach Chaim, sec. 139, para. 6) these are blessings said in vain, since they were instituted for the sake of the congregation.
Pele Yoetz 260:9: And the one called up must also read along in the Torah, reading quietly after the cantor, but should not raise his voice, since otherwise there is one who says his blessings would be in vain; and he should wait at the reader's table until the reading of the one called up after him is finished, and only then return to his place, while another is making a pledge, so as not to cause the congregation to stumble by interrupting with loud voices saying “Chazak baruch, chazak baruch,” to the point that the voice of the reading is not heard, and he himself also loses the reading due to the voice of the one speaking. And his ears should be attentive to the reading of the Torah scroll, letter by letter, word by word, with extra affection as though it were being given at Sinai, and he should not speak in the meantime, for it is a great sin and a criminal transgression; and certainly he should not leave the Torah scroll and go out, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 8a) that of him it is said, “And those who forsake the Lord shall be consumed” (Isaiah 1:28), Heaven have mercy. And let him consider that in every single word and every single stroke there are heaps upon heaps of supernal mysteries and secrets of secrets, and the work of our hands is established for us — happy are we, how good is our portion!
Pele Yoetz 260:10: Thus, how much more so is it incumbent upon the prayer leader to take to heart and give his life to be meticulous in reading the Torah portion with all its cantillation and precision as is proper, lacking nothing in it, for besides the fact that this is a disgraceful thing and he commits a transgression, and sometimes the meaning is changed and sometimes it turns out to be blasphemous, moreover it causes deficiency above according to the mystical meaning of the matter, and that man shall bear his sin. And the cantor who is careful in his reading, that it be a trustworthy reading, shall flourish like a cedar in Lebanon and like a rose.
Pele Yoetz 260:11: And a man whom the Lord has graced with wisdom and knowledge should compile a book, so that his wellsprings spread outward and his lips move in the grave, and thereby he acquires remembrance and a monument better than sons and daughters, and every wise man should act with knowledge and choose to make books that benefit the many, such as resolving the words of the Talmud and the early authorities, not for name or praise but only to adorn the bride, and likewise compile halachic rulings, and a pure man should gather collections and summaries of various kinds to benefit and bring merit to the many, and the merit of the many depends on him and on all who assist in printing them, for were it not for books and printing, Torah would have been forgotten from Israel, Heaven forbid. And let him precede with prayer before the Lord that nothing uncorrected come from his hand and that his wellsprings spread outward. And he should not worry if another has preceded him in some matter, for we find several prophets prophesying in the same style, and he too shall build upon it. And it is fitting for every author of a book to be careful and guard against sinning with his tongue in words of provocation, from which a sword and desecration of the Name result, and it is best not to speak of another book from good to bad, but rather write his own opinion and say, “See such-and-such a book,” and let the reader choose. Let the wise man hear and add learning.
Pele Yoetz 261:1: Sanegoria (Advocacy/Defense) — It is known that the Holy One, blessed be He, desires that people find merit in favor of Israel, both collectively and individually. And Elijah the Prophet, remembered for good, was punished for speaking accusation, saying (I Kings 19:14), “I have been very zealous for the Lord, the God of Hosts, for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant.” Likewise Isaiah the Prophet was punished for saying, “I dwell among a people of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). And greater than this we find that Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was punished for saying (Exodus 4:1), “But behold, they will not believe me.” And Gideon merited because he found merit in favor of Israel, and for this he merited to save Israel, as it is written (Judges 6:14), “Go in this your strength and save Israel.” And the reason is that whatever a person says leaves an impression and arouses the heavenly retinue — if he speaks accusation, he arouses the accusers; and if he speaks in defense, he arouses defenders, and his words bear fruit.
